characters: Tawia: a 14-year-old boy in a white shirt and grey trousers, with a notebook.
Rosina: his classmate, 14, in a school uniform with a headband, listening closely.
Mr Konney: their history teacher, in a plain shirt and spectacles, walking slowly.
Cape Coast Castle: a white castle on a rocky shore, with cannons facing the sea and a narrow doorway in its wall.

narrationPlan.voice: Quiet, steady voice with long pauses; Mr Konney speaks softly and carefully
narrationPlan.pace: Slow, quiet and respectful, with room to pause (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Very soft strings and distant waves; near silence for the dungeon page (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Cape Coast Castle is a World Heritage Site and a museum. This story uses published accounts and an invented teacher and pupils.
This is a serious subject. The story avoids graphic detail and shows learners using respectful language. Teachers should prepare for strong feelings and allow any learner to step out.
The names “Door of No Return” and “Door of Return” are used by guides and visitors; wording may differ between sources.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: Portuguese post in 1555 (Cabo Corso); Swedish lodge Carolusborg (1652 or 1653, sources differ); English capture in 1664; the dungeon by 1682 and its capacity (an estimate); restoration in the 1920s and early 1990s; Ghana Museums and Monuments Board from 1957; UNESCO 1979.
Ask the castle’s museum staff or the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board to review the wording, especially the “Door of Return” sentence.
Check that no sentence could read as blaming or shaming present-day learners or visitors.

teacherGuide.overview: A history story that treats the trade in enslaved people with dignity. It teaches respectful language, how historians handle uncertain dates and numbers, and why societies keep difficult places.
learningGoals: Describe how Cape Coast Castle changed hands and uses.
Explain why respectful language matters in history.
Explain why places of hard memory are kept.

subjectLinks.subject: Social Studies / History
subjectLinks.link: The Gold Coast and the Atlantic trade

beforeReading: Tell learners the story deals with a painful subject, that they may step out at any time, and that you will answer questions honestly.
whileReading: At page 5, discuss why the words we choose change how we think.
afterReading: Write a short, respectful sentence a visitor might write in a museum book.
Draw a timeline of the castle’s owners.
discussion: Why is it important to say “enslaved people” and not only “slaves”?
What does it mean to honour people from long ago?
reflection: How would you want a painful part of your own family’s past to be remembered?

mathsExtension.task: From the English capture in 1664 to Ghana’s independence in 1957 is how many years?
The Swedish lodge dates are given as 1652 or 1653. How many years to 2026 for each?

support: Give learners a short list of respectful words and let them practise using them aloud.
stretch: Research how other countries remember places linked to the trade in enslaved people.

whatWeKnow: The castle was held in turn by the Portuguese, Swedes, Dutch and English.
It was used to hold enslaved people before they were shipped across the Atlantic.
It is a museum and a World Heritage Site.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact date of the dungeon and the numbers it held at different times.
The year of the Swedish lodge, which sources give as 1652 or 1653.

factCheck.claim: Cape Coast Castle began as a Portuguese trading post in 1555; the Swedish Africa Company built the Carolusborg lodge in 1653 (another passage says 1652); the English captured it in 1664; it was a major holding site for enslaved Africans; the dungeon is estimated to date from 1682 and could hold about a thousand people; it was restored in the 1920s and early 1990s, and passed to the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board in 1957.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s Cape Coast Castle article, which itself flags the 1652 or 1653 uncertainty and says the dungeon’s date and capacity are estimates from secondary sources.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Cape Coast Castle”. Check also the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board and scholarly histories.

factCheck.claim: The castle is part of the UNESCO site “Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions”, inscribed in 1979.
